firm: Feel for a sharper tap or scrape than in silt. Repeat the drop and check for stones or crevices that could trap the lead.
Try a bottom bait or wafter on a simple, safe rig. A shorter hooklink can control presentation on even firm ground; adapt length and material to irregularities and ensure the lead cannot jam.
Start with a small scattered portion or a single hookbait under pressure. Add more only after feeding signs.
If weed is present, confirm a clean patch and safe landing route. Echo colour alone does not establish material.
soft: A lead may sink with a dull drop and return carrying sediment, plant remains or an odour. Check sediment depth; hook and hooklink may be buried.
A wafter or controlled low pop-up may remain clear of sediment. Use a safe lead setup and select hooklink length by testing how the rig lands, often longer than on firm bottom. Check local rig rules.
Begin with a few baits or a small patch. Check whether hookbait and feed sink into sediment before topping up.
Check any weed and the landing route. Soft bottom may still hold natural food; one sonar colour cannot tell you its quality.
weed: A lead may catch and retrieve plants. Repeat scans across the area, confirm a clean opening and a safe landing route with a lead.
On a verified clear opening, try a bottom bait or wafter. On an edge, use a suitable raised bait only when landing is safe. Match hooklink and lead release to weed height and local rules.
Place a small, precise portion on clear ground rather than scattering into dense growth. Increase after observed activity.
Check the clean patch and fish safety first. A single plant fragment does not describe an entire area.
structure: A lead may roll down a slope or catch on a shelf. Repeat tracks from two directions and check where the rig actually settles.
Use a bottom bait or wafter on a stable shelf or patch, adapting rig, hooklink and lead to snags. Ensure the lead can release safely.
Feed a small amount on a stable part, not a steep face. Confirm where the food lands before increasing it.
Check any weed, bottom type and safe landing route; structure shape alone is not a rig placement decision.

substrates: Gravel
firm
A strong rough scrape on the lead; often a thicker sonar return and sometimes a second echo.
A bottom bait or wafter after checking the drop. A short to medium hooklink and a little scattered feed are a starting point.
Stone and clay can also give strong returns; gravel is not proven by the echo alone.
Sand
firm
Even contact, often firmer than silt without gravel's distinctive scrape; a stable sonar line.
Try a bottom bait or wafter on a verified clean area.
Firm sand may look like other materials on screen.
Clay
firm
Smooth strong tap, sometimes clay residue on the lead; a clear echo does not reveal bottom chemistry.
Use a controlled bottom bait or wafter after feeling the area.
Hard clay can resemble gravel acoustically; check for sticky deposits.
Firm bottom
firm
Repeatable strong return, short hard landing and vibration on the retrieve.
Start with a controlled short to medium hooklink and confirm the actual descent.
Firm does not automatically mean gravel or natural food.
Light silt
soft
Weaker or thinner return, dull drop and a little sediment on the lead.
Consider a wafter or lighter lead. Set hooklink length after checking how far the lead sinks.
The hook can be partly covered even when the bait seems visible.
Deep silt
soft
Weak diffuse return; the lead sinks deeply and is hard to pull free.
Raise the hookbait above sediment or compare a firmer edge; verify a safe rig.
Both rig and food may disappear into the sediment.
Detritus
soft
Leaves and debris on the lead, uneven soft return and a variable layer above the real bottom.
Check whether a raised presentation can remain clear or move to a cleaner margin.
Rotting debris can hide the hook and change how bait smells.
Leaf litter
soft
Recognisable leaves on the lead; sonar may show only a soft layer.
Find a stable clean patch or keep hook and bait above the litter.
A single clean-looking return does not show how deep the leaf layer is.
Low weed
weed
An uneven low band above bottom; fine plants on the lead.
Match a wafter or low pop-up to actual height, targeting a gap or edge.
One retrieved plant fragment does not prove the entire patch is densely weedy.
Tall weed
weed
Plants extend into the water column at varying heights on repeat scans.
Prefer a large clear opening or outer edge with a safe landing route.
A rig placed inside dense stems can be unsafe even if fish marks appear nearby.
Pondweed
weed
Complex, sometimes tall plants; identify from a retrieved fragment or visual check, not sonar alone.
Map a clear corridor or outside edge and check landing safety.
Similar plants can give the same echo shape.
Elodea
weed
Fine dense aquatic plants; the image resembles other submerged weed.
Find a verified gap large enough for repeatable placement.
Sonar cannot reliably establish plant species.
Dead weed / chod
soft
Soft irregular layer and dead plant fragments on the lead.
Test a safe raised presentation only if permitted and the lead can release; compare a cleaner edge.
Dead weed can conceal the hook and create snags.
Gravel to silt
soft
Repeatable change in echo strength and lead feel over a short distance.
Compare both sides and verify which one receives the lead and hookbait.
Beam width and movement blur the exact boundary on screen.
Weed edge
weed
Sudden reduction in plant height on repeat parallel tracks.
Target the clear side or a checked gap, allowing for GPS and beam error.
An apparently precise line may be displaced from the true edge.
Clear hole
weed
A short gap among plants recurring on several passes; verify with a marker.
Place a bottom bait, wafter or small PVA precisely if the gap is large enough.
GPS and cone width introduce error; the rig may land on the weedy rim.
Plateau
structure
A relatively flat area after a depth change; it need not have hard bottom.
Compare the top with its edge and base, then check bottom and fish signs.
A flat screen during a stopped scan is not proof of a plateau.
Drop or ledge
structure
A repeatable depth change on passes in opposite directions.
Test a stable upper or lower edge depending on fish, food and presentation.
A wide beam can conceal a steep face or make the hooklink hang.
Channel or trough
structure
A local hollow repeated on several cross tracks.
Compare entrance, firm side and base after checking silt and oxygen.
The deepest point is not automatically the best or safest.
Underwater hump
structure
Depth rises and falls when crossing from several directions.
Compare top, side and base, then confirm firmness and a safe landing route.
A strong return on top does not prove fish or natural food.

food: No flavour has a reliable exclusive temperature band. Below 16°C start with less food; at 16–24°C follow actual activity; above 24°C prioritise oxygen and fish welfare. Under pressure compare a small neutral hookbait.
Use a bottom bait on clean ground, a balanced wafter over light sediment, or a pop-up if weed requires lift. Match hooklink length and material to the actual bottom.
Test a single hookbait first; after confirming fish, start with a small portion of related food and increase only after a response.
If fish are present without taking, compare a small neutral wafter and one contrasting bait. Never credit flavour alone without controlling spot, amount, size and colour.
spice: No reliable season or temperature belongs to this flavour alone. Start with less food in cool water and adjust to feeding; heat makes oxygen and welfare the priority.
Compare bottom bait and wafter at the same location. Raise a pop-up only when weed or sediment requires it; choose hooklink to fit the bottom.
Start with a single hookbait or a few small portions. Increase only after activity.
If the strong signal changes nothing, compare a neutral bait, size and rig location instead of adding more flavour.
sweet: There is no reliable temperature window for this profile. Reduce food in cool water, follow feeding in warmer water and prioritise oxygen during heat.
Try a bottom bait on confirmed ground, a wafter for a lighter presentation or a pop-up when bottom is uncertain. Match hooklink and lead to conditions.
A single hookbait is a useful pressured-water test. When feeding is confirmed, compare a small rule-permitted food patch.
With no response, compare a neutral smaller bait and less feed before blaming the flavour.
fruit: Fruit has no guaranteed seasonal window. In cool water use less food; in warmth follow fish activity; in heat put oxygen and welfare first.
Compare a natural bottom bait with a small fruit wafter or pop-up on a separate rig, controlling colour and buoyancy.
Start with a single hookbait. Feed a small amount only after activity; hookbait flavour need not match every free bait.
If a bright contrast fails under pressure, try a smaller bait in a natural colour. Keep location and food amount comparable.
natural: No fixed seasonal window. Observe temperature and fish activity, reduce food in cold water and prioritise oxygen in heat.
Use worms, larvae or unscented particles only where rules allow them, with a rig suitable for nuisance fish and the actual bottom.
Offer a small amount of properly prepared food; never scatter uncooked particles.
If small fish dominate, choose a more selective hookbait and reduce fine food.

It cannot fix poor rig presentation.
Avoid changing feed and colour simultaneously.
Test alongside feed amount and colour.
Do not infer a season from the name.
Aroma strength does not prove feeding value.
Follow particle preparation and lake rules.
Actual tiger nuts must be prepared safely.
Colour and buoyancy may matter more than aroma.

Do not add several new signals at once.
A flavour name is not a feeding forecast.
Match hookbait size and colour in the test.
temperatures: Use little food and locate fish patiently. Slower metabolism does not mean feeding stops.
Small patches, check more stable areas and watch the direction of temperature change.
Compare sun-warmed shallows with safe deeper water; increase food only after a response.
Activity may rise on many waters. Observe fish and local trends before feeding more.
Spawning may occur. Leave spawning fish undisturbed and obey closures.
Activity can be high, but adjust food to stock, actual feeding and oxygen.
Oxygen and fish welfare take priority over bite counts; minimise stress.
